title: The Forecast Miss

scenario.situation: The demand-forecast model's mean absolute error tripled last week, triggering an alert. The analytics lead wants an emergency retrain before the next peak period.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The analytics lead is convinced the model has degraded — weights have drifted, data pipelines shifted, or something inside the model broke — and that retraining immediately is the only fix.
scenario.question: Has the model actually degraded, or is something else driving the error spike?

decisions.prompt: Before touching the model, how do you structure your investigation?

options.label: Audit the model internals for drift
options.detail: Check feature importances, weight distributions, and pipeline logs for signs of model or data drift.
options.consequence: You spend a day inspecting the model and find nothing obviously broken inside — because nothing is. The investigation stalls and you're no closer to understanding why errors spiked.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the degradation hypothesis and searched inside the model when the cause was outside it.

options.label: Diagnostic slicing by input conditions
options.detail: Slice forecast errors by the conditions under which predictions were made — day type, temperature band, season — to see whether the error is uniform or concentrated.
options.consequence: Errors cluster sharply in a specific temperature band corresponding to last week's heatwave. On all other days the model is accurate. The pattern points away from model rot and toward an out-of-distribution input regime.

options.label: Immediately retrain on the most recent data
options.detail: Add last week's data to the training set and retrain the model right away.
options.consequence: The retrained model fits last week well but overweights the anomalous heatwave period. On typical days, accuracy actually worsens — you've introduced overfitting while fixing nothing structural.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to a solution before diagnosing the problem, risking overfitting to an anomaly.

options.label: Compare this week's error to historical error distributions
options.detail: Pull the model's MAE over the past 12 months and see if last week is a statistical outlier.
options.consequence: Last week's error is obviously an outlier — you already knew that from the alert. The historical comparison confirms severity but tells you nothing about why it happened or whether the model is at fault.
options.divergenceCost: Confirmed the symptom already known from the alert without advancing toward the cause.

decisions.prompt: You've sliced errors by temperature band. Which metric do you rely on to determine whether the model is broken or simply out of range?

artifact.title: Total forecast error (MWh) by temperature band — last 30 days
artifact.caption: Raw total error MWh per band. The heatwave band dominates — but heatwave days also had the highest demand. Is the model bad here, or just stretched far beyond its range?

options.label: Total absolute error (MWh) by temperature band
options.detail: Sum the raw forecast errors within each temperature band.
options.consequence: The heatwave band shows by far the most total error — but heatwave days also had record-high demand. The raw error is large partly because the numbers themselves are large. You can't tell if the model is proportionally worse or just operating at greater scale.
options.divergenceCost: Compared raw error volumes across bands with very different demand scales — a classic size confound.

options.label: Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) by temperature band
options.detail: Normalize forecast error as a percentage of actual demand within each band.
options.consequence: Normalized, the story is unmistakable: MAPE in the sub-95°F bands is stable at 2–4%, consistent with historical performance. In the 95°F+ band — temperatures the model has seen fewer than five times in training — MAPE spikes to 31%. The model isn't broken; it's extrapolating wildly outside its training distribution.

artifact.title: Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) by temperature band — last 30 days
artifact.caption: Normalized to actual demand, the heatwave band's error dwarfs all others. Every other band is performing within normal historical range — the model is fine; last week's temperatures were not.

decisions.prompt: MAPE is high only in the extreme-heat band, which the model has rarely seen in training. What do you tell the analytics lead?

options.label: "It's the heatwave, not model rot — no retrain needed."
options.detail: Assert the cause confidently and recommend closing the retrain request.
options.consequence: You've stated a plausible finding but made a definitive causal claim from a single week of data. If there's also a subtle pipeline issue coinciding with the heatwave, you've given the analytics lead false certainty and a reason to skip a more careful validation.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty from a correlation, foreclosing further validation that could catch a real secondary issue.

options.label: "The error concentrates entirely in the extreme-heat band — temperatures rarely seen in training. On all other days the model is normal. Retraining on one anomalous week risks overfitting; I'd recommend validating on the next hot period and, if we expect more extreme heat, augmenting training data deliberately rather than emergency-retraining now."
options.detail: Share the finding, flag the extrapolation mechanism, advise against immediate retrain, and propose a deliberate path forward.
options.consequence: The analytics lead now has a concrete, evidence-based reframe: the model isn't broken, the inputs were out of range. You've also given a credible alternative action — deliberate data augmentation — and a validation trigger, turning a panic retrain into a measured improvement plan.

insight: The forecast miss had nothing to do with model degradation — the model performed normally on every day within its training distribution; it only failed at temperatures it had almost never seen. Retraining on a single anomalous week would have overfit the model to an extreme event and degraded everyday accuracy. The core lesson is distribution shift versus model rot: before retraining, a sound analyst checks whether the inputs themselves moved out of range, not just whether the error got larger. Distinguishing an extrapolation failure from a degradation failure requires normalizing error by scale and slicing by input conditions — the same diagnostic instinct that prevents the most expensive kind of model 'fix.'
